title: Human-in-the-loop in workflows
summary: An executor sends a typed request out of the workflow and waits. The caller answers with a response, and the framework routes it back. Pending requests are saved in checkpoints and re-emitted on restore, so the wait can outlive the process.
useIf: A step needs a person or an external system to decide, approve or supply data before the graph continues.
avoidIf: The decision is one tool approval inside a single chat turn: a tool-level approval with the same session is simpler.

explain.md: **.NET and Go:** create a `RequestPort` (for example `RequestPort.Create<NumberSignal, int>("GuessNumber")`), add it to the graph; messages sent to it emit a `RequestInfoEvent`, and you reply with `handle.SendResponseAsync(evt.Request.CreateResponse(value))`. **Python:** an executor calls `await ctx.request_info(request_data=..., response_type=...)` and handles the answer in a method decorated with `@response_handler`. The caller sees an event with `type == "request_info"` and resumes with `workflow.run(responses={request_id: answer}, stream=True)` (this replaced `send_responses*` in 1.0.0b260210) [[tr19]].

**Durability.** When a checkpoint is created, pending requests are saved with it. On restore they are re-emitted as request events. You can pass `checkpoint_id` and `responses` in one `run(...)` call to resume and answer together [[tr19]]. **In orchestrations**, tool approvals arrive through the same mechanism with `function_approval_request` content (Python) or `ToolApprovalRequestContent` (.NET). Handoff is interactive by default and returns control to the user when an agent does not hand off; sequential, concurrent and group chat do not pause for free text on their own, so pair them with a `RequestPort` in a custom graph when you need that control [[tr19]] [[tr25]].

explain.title: Request, wait, resume
explain.alt: An executor raises a request, the workflow pauses and saves a checkpoint, a human responds later, and the workflow resumes from the checkpoint with the response.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as Executor
  participant W as Workflow
  participant C as Checkpoint store
  participant H as Human
  E->>W: request_info(question)
  W->>C: save pending request
  W-->>H: request_info event
  H->>W: run(checkpoint_id, responses)
  W->>E: response_handler(answer)

whereToUse: Manager sign-off on refunds, payouts or deployments
Collecting missing data from a user mid-process
Reviewing a Magentic plan before agents start (`MagenticPlanReviewRequest`)
Approving tool calls made by agents inside orchestrations
Pausing a durable workflow for days without paying for idle compute (Durable Extension)

use: The approver may answer later or from another system
The wait must survive restarts, so pending state must be checkpointed
You need typed requests and a record of who answered what
avoid: A quick yes or no inside an open chat: a tool approval with the same session is enough
Approvals every few seconds: batch them or tighten the tool scope
Treating a request id as an authorisation: verify the responder's identity yourself
flips: Approvers answer in free text rather than yes or no: use handoff (interactive by default) or a request port with a richer response type
The wait is days and compute must be zero: run on the Durable Extension, where a workflow waits without consuming compute or tokens

pitfalls.symptom: Resume re-emits a request that was already answered
pitfalls.cause: The response was not delivered in the same call or checkpoint lineage, so the pending request is restored
pitfalls.fix: Resume with `checkpoint_id` and `responses` together, and track request ids you answered

pitfalls.symptom: Python 1.0 samples with `RequestInfoExecutor` or `send_responses` do not run
pitfalls.cause: The concepts page and older samples differ from the HITL page; `send_responses*` was replaced by `run(responses=...)`
pitfalls.fix: Follow the HITL page, which has working graph-executor code

pitfalls.symptom: Approvals from sequential or group chat never ask for free text
pitfalls.cause: Those orchestrations do not pause for free text on their own
pitfalls.fix: Use handoff, or add a `RequestPort` executor in a custom workflow

scenarios.title: Manager approves overnight
scenarios.situation: A procurement workflow raises a request for a manager. The manager answers the next morning from a different web app. The service restarts nightly.
unknowns: How does the web app know the request id?
What if the manager never answers?
scenarios.question: How do you implement the wait?

options.name: Request port (or `request_info`) with durable checkpoint storage; the web app stores the request id and later resumes with `checkpoint_id` and `responses`
options.why: Pending requests persist and are re-emitted on restore, independent of the process.
options.tradeoff: You build the inbox, id handling and a timeout path.

options.name: Block the executor on an in-memory future
options.why: Lost on restart and holds resources for hours.
options.tradeoff: Fine for sub-minute waits in a demo.

options.name: Poll a database from a loop inside the executor
options.why: Simple, and survives if the executor reruns idempotently.
options.tradeoff: Holds compute while waiting and bypasses the framework's request model.

flips.if: Waits are days and compute costs matter
flips.then: Run on the Durable Extension with `wait_for_external_event` and a timer.
Persist the request yourself and restart the graph from that point.

scenarios.takeaway: A request survives restarts only if its checkpoint does.

scenarios.title: Approvals inside a group chat
scenarios.situation: A group chat of three agents drafts an announcement. One agent has a publish tool that needs approval. A moderator should be able to approve in the same UI session within minutes.
unknowns: Is the UI a web socket or request-response?
scenarios.question: How do approvals reach the moderator?

options.name: Handle the request event carrying the approval content from the orchestration stream, and reply with the response
options.why: Tool approvals in orchestrations arrive as request events through the HITL mechanism, with no extra graph.
options.tradeoff: The UI must keep the run attached or checkpoint it.

options.name: Disable approval on the publish tool
options.why: Removes the control that protects publishing.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only for a draft-only tool.

options.name: Add a free-text pause between rounds
options.why: Gives a moderator a say each round.
options.tradeoff: Group chat does not pause for free text on its own, so you need a custom graph.

flips.then: Add checkpoint storage so the pending request persists.

flips.if: Several tools need approval in one batch
flips.then: Collect all decisions; no tool runs until the whole batch is decided.

scenarios.takeaway: Approvals ride the same request channel, whatever the orchestration.

quiz.q: Order the Python request and resume flow.
items: Caller gathers the answer for each `request_id`
quiz.explain: Requests surface as events, answers are keyed by request id, and the framework routes each answer to the executor's response handler. Pending requests are stored in checkpoints.

quiz.q: Which orchestration returns control to the user by default when an agent does not hand off?
quiz.explain: Handoff is interactive by default. Sequential, concurrent and group chat do not pause for free text on their own.

flashcards.front: How do .NET and Python differ in raising a request?
flashcards.back: .NET and Go: a `RequestPort` emitting `RequestInfoEvent`. Python: `ctx.request_info(...)` plus an `@response_handler` method.

flashcards.front: What happens to a pending request at a checkpoint?
flashcards.back: It is saved with the checkpoint and re-emitted as a request event on restore. You can resume and answer in one call.

flashcards.front: How are tool approvals surfaced inside orchestrations?
flashcards.back: As request events carrying `function_approval_request` content (Python) or `ToolApprovalRequestContent` (.NET).
